chapter.title: Meet the builder: the terminal and your first request

cards.body: You've hired a builder, but they won't start until you walk them to the plot of land. The terminal is the front gate where you meet them. The folder you open it in is the plot. Everything the builder makes goes on that plot, and nowhere else.

cards.title: The terminal is a text window, the folder is the plot
cards.body:
The terminal is a window where you type a command and press Enter instead of clicking. On a Mac, press Cmd+Space, type Terminal, press Enter. A blank window with a blinking cursor appears. That blink means it is waiting for you.

A folder in the terminal is the same folder you see in Finder. The terminal is always standing inside one folder. Type pwd (print working directory) and press Enter to see which one.

To make a new folder, type mkdir hello-page (make directory). To step into it, type cd hello-page (change directory). Now pwd ends in hello-page. You are standing on the plot.

Claude Code is a program you start from the terminal by typing claude and pressing Enter. It works only inside the folder you were standing in. That one rule decides where your files land, so check pwd first.

To install it, open the Claude Code install page in the official docs, copy the one install line, paste it in the terminal, press Enter. The first time you type claude, it asks you to sign in with your Claude account in the browser.

cards.prompt: You open Terminal, it is standing in your Downloads folder, you type claude and ask for a one-page site. Where does the new file land?

options.text: In Downloads, because that is where the terminal was standing
On the Desktop, so you can see it

whyNot.b: That's where you might look for it, not where the builder works: the builder only builds on the plot you walked them to.
whyNot.c: That's the builder picking the plot, which never happens: you pick it by where the terminal is standing when you type claude.

cards.reteach: Claude Code is tied to one folder: the one the terminal is in at the moment you start it. It reads and writes there. If you want files in hello-page, step into hello-page with cd before typing claude.

cards.title: One page, two minutes
cards.body:
Sam makes a folder with mkdir hello-page, steps in with cd hello-page, and types claude. After sign-in, Sam types: "Make one file called index.html that shows the words Hello, Sam in big letters. Then open it in my browser."

Claude says it will create index.html and shows the plan. It asks for a yes before writing the file. Sam presses Enter to allow it. A browser tab opens with Hello, Sam in large text.

That is the whole first job: 1 folder, 1 file, 1 request, and Sam saw it work with their own eyes.

cards.title: Say yes on purpose, then look with your own eyes
cards.body:
Before Claude writes or changes a file, it stops and asks. Read the one line that says what it wants to do. If it matches what you asked, allow it. If not, type no and say what you meant. You hold the keys; the builder does not get in without you.

Claude then tells you what it did in plain words. Do not take its word for it. Open the file or the browser tab and check. A first request should be something you can see in under a minute, like a page with your name on it.

When you are done, type /exit to leave Claude Code and get back to the normal terminal. Your folder and files stay exactly where they are.

cards.prompt: Which first request fits this chapter's rule, something tiny you can see work?

options.text: Build me a budgeting app with sign-in and charts.
Make one page that says Hello, Priya in big letters and open it in my browser.

whyNot.a: That's a whole house, not a first visit to the plot: there are 3 or 4 jobs in there and nothing you can check in a minute.
whyNot.c: That's a chat, not a build: nothing appears in your folder, so there is nothing to see work.

cards.reteach: The first request has one job and one thing to look at. One file, one visible result, under a minute. You are testing that the builder, the plot, and your eyes all line up, not building the house yet.

cards.body: People type claude from their home folder or the Desktop, where hundreds of unrelated files live. Claude then reads things it should not and drops new files in a mess. Spot it: when Claude Code starts, it shows the folder path at the top. If that path does not end in the project folder you meant, type /exit, cd into the right folder, and start again.

cards.prompt: What decides where Claude Code reads and writes files?

options.text: The folder the terminal is standing in when you type claude
The words you use in your request

whyNot.b: That's what gets built, not where: the request is the work order, the folder is the plot.
whyNot.c: That's where you look at the result, not where it is stored: the browser only shows the file that already landed in the folder.

cards.reteach: Think of the terminal as standing on one square of ground. Type pwd to see which square. Claude builds on that square and only that square. Move first with cd, then start the builder.

cards.body: Open Terminal. Type mkdir first-build, then cd first-build, then claude. Ask for one page that shows your name and today's date, opened in your browser. Then type /exit.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now start Claude Code inside a folder you chose, make one plain-English request, and see the file it built open in your browser.
